text: System Administration Lesson 9 introduced security_admin as a troubleshooting detail: editing an ACL record requires elevating through Elevate Roles, because sys_security_acl has its own ACLs that even a full admin doesn't bypass by default. This lesson treats it as what it actually is — one of the most consequential privilege boundaries on the platform.

Here's the detail that makes it genuinely dangerous: when security_admin is active, ACL script evaluation is bypassed specifically for edits to ACL records themselves. Every other ACL, on every other table, still runs normally for every other user and operation. The bypass is narrow and sharp.

That narrowness is exactly why it's so powerful. ACLs are the rules that govern what every role, user, and table can do across the whole instance. A careless or malicious edit made while that bypass is active doesn't just change one record — it changes the rules deciding behavior everywhere else.

That's why security_admin is deliberately not always-on, even for full admins. Permanently granting it would mean every admin session — checking a ticket, updating a record — carries a live, standing ability to rewrite platform-wide access rules. Elevate Roles narrows that window on purpose: active only for the current session, only when explicitly turned on.

Scoping when the bypass is active only solves half the problem. The real governance practice is treating the elevation event itself as worth tracking — logging every elevation, and alerting a security team when one happens, the same way a bank logs every time a vault is opened rather than only restricting who holds a key.

If an account elevates to security_admin at 2 a.m., or an account that rarely touches ACLs suddenly edits several in a row, that's a signal worth a human looking at — not an event that passes by unnoticed just because the user technically had the right to elevate.

This is a concrete instance of a question every layered access-control system has to answer: what stops the mechanism that enforces the rules from being quietly rewritten by someone with just enough access to reach it. Next, Lesson 19 covers how ServiceNow's own audit logging tracks changes like these.
